newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Copper recycling bound up by red tape - US academic.
newsitem.headline: Copper recycling bound up by red tape - US academic.

text.p: Excessive regulation based on mistaken ideas about copper recycling could disrupt the industry, Robert Frosch, a leading American industrial ecology academic said on Monday.
Frosch, a senior fellow of Harvard University and of the National Academy of Engineering, said severe penalties against hazardous waste risked undermining a highly efficient industry.
"We must be very careful if we mess around," Frosch told Reuters after addressing a two-day world conference on copper recycling organised by the Lisbon-based International Copper Study Group.
Copper intended for recycling should not be regarded as "waste" but should be put into a more respectable category, he said.

The hazardous waste tag on copper discouraged U.S. smelters from recycling the metal which was sent across to Canada. A 90-day recycling deadline also encouraged U.S. operators to get rid of the metal.
Frosch earlier told the conference that a survey of 64 copper firms in Massachusetts, USA, found that only about one percent of copper was lost annually in emissions or landfill.
Cost and the fear of liability were powerful incentives to recycle the metal, he said.

On the other hand 50 percent of copper used by consumers was not recycled, he noted. Cars, clothes washers and computers were among items disposed of in landfill sites. --Peter Blackburn Brussels Bureau +322 287 6830
